### Problem: Distinct subsequences II {#sec-lis-p5-dist}

::: {.p-statement}
Given a string `s` of lowercase letters, return the number of distinct non-empty subsequences, modulo $10^9 + 7$. Two subsequences that spell the same string are the same answer, even when they use different indices.

$1 \le |s| \le 2000$ in the quadratic view; the last-letter scan is linear and handles $10^5$. `"abc"` answers 7. `"aba"` answers 6. `"aaa"` answers 3, not 7: the seven position sets spell only `a`, `aa`, and `aaa`.

Source: [LC 940 · Distinct Subsequences II](https://leetcode.com/problems/distinct-subsequences-ii/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
New letter $c$ can be appended to every distinct subsequence already counted, and it can also start the one-letter string $c$. That doubles the collection, including a slot for the empty string that we do not return. The subsequences that already ended with an earlier $c$ are generated again, so subtract the count that the previous $c$ was responsible for. `"aaa"` stays at 3. Adding instead of replacing would count position sets.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
- **State.** $end[c]$ = number of distinct subsequences, over the prefix read so far, that end with letter $c$. `total` includes the empty subsequence and starts at 1.
- **Transition.** Let `old = end[c]`. Set `end[c] = total`, then `total = 2 * total - old`. Appending $c$ to everything in `total` adds `total` new strings and retires the `old` ones that this letter already produced.
- **Answer.** `total - 1`, modulo $10^9 + 7$. The empty string is the subtracted 1.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Why aaa has three strings and seven position sets"}
The position sets of `"aaa"` are the seven non-empty subsets of three indices. They spell `a` three ways, `aa` three ways, and `aaa` one way. The problem asks for strings. After the first `a`, `end['a'] = 1` and one non-empty string exists. The second `a` would double that collection and then subtract the previous `end['a']`, leaving `a` and `aa`. The third letter leaves `a`, `aa`, `aaa`. A count of index sets is the number-of-LIS pair, not this scan.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Enumeration

::: {.form-next}
Every subset of positions spells a string. A set collects them and drops the empty string. This is the definition, and it is $2^n$. It is here to check the three samples, not to run on a long string.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("dist", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "7"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: dist-rec
def dist_rec(s):
    found = set()

    def f(i, cur):
        if i == len(s):
            if cur:
                found.add(cur)
            return
        f(i + 1, cur)
        f(i + 1, cur + s[i])

    f(0, "")
    return len(found)
```

##### C++

```cpp
void distWalk(int i, string cur, const string& s, set<string>& found) {
    if (i == (int)s.size()) {
        if (!cur.empty()) found.insert(cur);
        return;
    }
    distWalk(i + 1, cur, s, found);
    distWalk(i + 1, cur + s[i], s, found);
}
```
:::

#### Memo on the letter

::: {.form-next}
The enumeration repeats the same suffix for many prefixes that spell the same string. The linear scan below is the memoised form of "what does a letter append": each letter stores how many distinct strings currently end with it, which is exactly the set of strings the enumeration would have inserted.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("dist", "memo")
    assert str(final) == "7"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: dist-memo
def dist_memo(s):
    end = {}
    total = 1
    for ch in s:
        old = end.get(ch, 0)
        end[ch] = total
        total = (total + end[ch] - old) % MOD
    return (total - 1) % MOD
```

##### C++

```cpp
int distMemo(const string& s) {
    const int MOD = 1000000007;
    long long end[26] = {}, total = 1;
    for (char ch : s) {
        int c = ch - 'a';
        long long old = end[c];
        end[c] = total;
        total = (total + end[c] - old + MOD) % MOD;
    }
    return (total - 1 + MOD) % MOD;
}
```
:::

#### Last letter

::: {.form-next}
`end[c]` is replaced, not added. Setting it to `total` means "every string so far, including empty, gains a copy that ends with `c`". Subtracting the previous `end[c]` removes the copies this letter had already contributed. The answer drops the empty string.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("dist", "tab")
    assert str(final) == "7"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: dist-tab
def dist_tab(s):
    end = [0] * 26
    total = 1
    for ch in s:
        c = ord(ch) - 97
        old = end[c]
        end[c] = total
        total = (total + end[c] - old) % MOD
    return (total - 1) % MOD
```

##### C++

```cpp
int distTab(const string& s) {
    const int MOD = 1000000007;
    long long end[26] = {}, total = 1;
    for (char ch : s) {
        int c = ch - 'a';
        long long old = end[c];
        end[c] = total;
        total = (total + total - old + MOD) % MOD;
    }
    return (total - 1 + MOD) % MOD;
}
```
:::

#### Subtract the old end

::: {.form-next}
The same numbers, written as a doubling. `new total = 2 * total - old`, where `old` is the count stored for this letter before the write. `"abc"` doubles three times and never subtracts a positive old count, so the non-empty answer is $8 - 1 = 7$. `"aba"` subtracts the first `a` when the second `a` arrives, and the answer is 6.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("dist", "last")
    assert str(final) == "7"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: dist-last
def dist_last(s):
    return dist_tab(s)

assert dist_rec("abc") == dist_memo("abc") == dist_tab("abc") == dist_last("abc") == 7
assert dist_rec("aba") == dist_tab("aba") == 6
assert dist_rec("aaa") == dist_tab("aaa") == 3
assert dist_tab("a") == 1
assert dist_tab("ab") == 3
```

##### C++

```cpp
int distinctSubseqII(const string& s) {
    const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;
    long long end[26] = {}, total = 1;                 // total counts the empty subsequence too
    for (char ch : s) {
        long long old = end[ch - 'a'];
        end[ch - 'a'] = total;
        total = ((2 * total - old) % MOD + MOD) % MOD;
    }
    return (int)((total - 1 + MOD) % MOD);
}
```
:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Enumeration** is $O(2^n \cdot n)$ with the string copies, and only the samples use it. The **last-letter** scan is $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ memory for a fixed alphabet, or $O(n)$ memory if the alphabet is large and you use a map. Every arithmetic step is modulo $10^9 + 7$. Subtracting `old` can go negative before the modulus; add the modulus before reducing.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- One letter: the answer is 1.
- Two different letters: `a`, `b`, `ab`, three strings.
- A letter repeated $n$ times: the answer is $n$, one string of each length. It is not $2^n - 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Counting position sets. `"aaa"` has seven non-empty subsets and three strings. The sample is the test that catches the add-instead-of-replace bug.
- Including the empty string. `total` starts at 1 so that a first letter has something to append to. The returned value is `total - 1`.
- A negative residue. `(2 * total - old) % MOD` in Python is fine when the language's remainder is non-negative. In C++ add `MOD` before the `%`.
:::

**Variants.** Binary strings, distinct, and no leading zero except the string `0` itself, is this scan with the extra string `"0"`: [LC 1987 · Number of Unique Good Subsequences](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-unique-good-subsequences/){difficulty="Hard"}. Buying the longest distinct subsequences first, for a limited budget, is the same count per length: [CF 1183H · Subsequences (hard version)](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1183/H){rating="1900"}. Distinct subsequences that are substrings of a second string, with no two taken from adjacent positions, is the same last-letter idea on a tighter alphabet: [AC abc214_f · Substrings](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc214/tasks/abc214_f). Counting the position sets that spell one fixed target is a different problem, a walk that matches the target letter by letter: [LC 115 · Distinct Subsequences](https://leetcode.com/problems/distinct-subsequences/){difficulty="Hard"}.
